title: Cc Ni Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala vs . Gurpreet Singh Page No. 1 on 11 May, 2023
full_text: Cc Ni Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala vs . Gurpreet Singh Page No. 1 on 11 May, 2023 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 1 IN THE COURT OF MS. AISHWARYA SHARMA, METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE (NI ACT) DIGITAL COURT­02, SOUTH­EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURT COMPLEX, NEW DELHI Criminal Complaint No: CC NI ACT/7822/2021 RAJ BALA ... Complainant Versus GURPREET SINGH ... Accused 1. Name & address of the complainant: Smt. Raj Bala W/O Sh. Sultan Singh R/O 838, Main Road Ekat Vihar Near Hanuman Builder, Meethapur Ext. New Delhi­110044 2. Name & address of the accused : Sh. Gurpreet Singh R/O Kailash Vatika, DDA, Community Hall Center Near Hare Rama Hare Krishna Mandir, New Delhi­110065 3. Offence complained of : U/S 138, The Negotiable Instruments Act,1881 . 4. Plea of accused : Pleaded not guilty. 5. Final Arguments : 27.04.2023 6. Date of Institution of case : 04.10.2021 7. Date of decision of the case : 11.05.2023 JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this court shall dispose of the aforementioned Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:03:58 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 2 complaint case filed by Smt. Raj Bala (hereinafter referred to as the 'complainant') against Sh. Gurpreet Singh (hereinafter referred to as the 'accused'). 2. Factual Matrix: The complainant's case is that the complainant knew the accused through a common friend and the accused availed friendly loan of Rs. 35,000/­ on 19.11.2019 for a period of one year on account of some financial crisis. It is stated that at the time of obtaining this loan in discharge of his legal liability for repayment of the loan amount, the accused had given one post­dated cheque bearing No. 000011 dated 20.11.2020 for a sum of Rs. 35,000/­ drawn on Bank of Baroda, Defence Colony Branch, New Delhi (hereinafter referred to as the "cheque in question") with the assurance that the same will be honoured upon it's presentation. However, when this cheque was presented by the complainant, it was dishonoured for the reason "FUNDS INSUFFICIENT" vide return memo dated 21.11.2020. Thereafter, the complainant sent a legal demand notice dated 17.12.2020 U/S 138 of the N.I. Act through whatsapp message sent on 18.12.2020, asking the accused to make the payment of the cheque amount, which was duly served upon the accused, however, he failed to make the payment despite delivery of the legal demand notice. It is further stated that the notice was sent to accused through Whatsapp as the accused has left his previous rented house and did not inform the complainant about his new address. Hence, being aggrieved, the complainant has filed the present complaint under section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 on 04.10.2021 and prayed that the accused be summoned, tried and punished under section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 3. Summoning of accused: This court summoned the accused after hearing the arguments at the stage of pre­summoning vide order dated 17.01.2022 and the accused entered appearance in the present case on 10.02.2023 and he was granted bail on the same date. Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:04:17 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 3 4. Notice: The court has framed notice of accusation under Section 251 Cr.P.C. against the accused on 12.04.2023. The substance of accusation was read over and explained to the accused and after being satisfied that the accused comprehended the same, the court recorded his plea. 5. Plea of the accused: The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. The accused admitted his signatures on the cheque in question, however, denied filling it's particulars. He denied receiving of the legal demand notice at his address through post and stated that he was working at this address till March, 2020 and thereafter, he left his job and further stated that the his correct address is 307/18, K Block, Sangam Vihar, New Delhi­110062. However, he admitted that he has received the legal demand notice through whatsapp on his mobile number 9891638489. He further stated that he intends to make the payment to the complainant, however, he requires sometime for doing the same. On the same date, the statement of admission and denial was also recorded U/S 294 Cr. P.C wherein, the accused admitted the correctness of dishonour memo, pursuant to which Bank Witnesses at Sr. No. 2 & 3 were dropped. 6. Evidence on behalf of complainant: To prove her case prima facie, the complainant has filed her evidence under Section 200 of the Cr.P.C. by way of an affidavit EX. CW 1/E wherein she has reiterated the averments made in the complaint. To prove her case, the complainant has also relied upon the original cheque dated 20.11.2020 EX. CW1/A, the return memo dated 21.11.2020 EX.CW1/B, the legal demand notice EX. CW1/C dated 17.12.2020 along with it's proof of delivery through whats app message. Thereafter, the complainant was subjected to cross­examination. 7. During her cross­examination, the complainant stated that she knows the accused through one common friend namely Mrs. Pooja, who is residing on rent near Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:04:26 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 4 her premise. She stated that she knew Mrs. Pooja since last 3­4 years as MR. Rahul, who is the husband of Mrs. Pooja is friend of her husband. She further stated that accused approached her through Mrs. Pooja for a friendly loan of Rs.35,000/­. She stated that she had not given any loan to any other person at the instance of Mrs. Pooja. She stated that she was initially not willing to give any friendly loan, but the accused assured her to give his post dated cheque for the said loan, thus, she agreed to give the loan amount to the accused. She stated that she had given the loan amount to the accused in cash. She further deposed that she used to earn by doing stitching work at home. She also stated that she was having an amount of Rs.15,000/­ with her and had borrowed Rs.20,000/­ from her friends at interest @2 % per annum and thus, advanced the amount of Rs.35,000/­ to the accused. Thereafter, the CE was closed vide separate statement of complainant vide separate statement of complainant recorded on 27.04.2023. 8. Examination of the accused under section 313 Cr.P.C.: The accused was examined under section 313 Cr.P.C. on 27.04.2023 wherein the accused admitted that he had taken friendly loan of Rs.35,000/­ from the complainant in the year 2019 as he knew the complainant through their common friend namely Mrs. Pooja. However, the accused stated that this amount was not given for one year and there was no time fixed for return of the amount. He admitted that at the time of obtaining this loan, he had given one blank post dated cheque i.e. EX CW­1/A i.e. cheque in question to the complainant however, he stated that the cheque in question was given as a security to assure the return of the loan amount taken from the complainant. He also admitted the correctness of dishonour memo EX. CW1/B and further, stated that at that time he did not have sufficient balance in his account due to lockdown. He also admitted that he received the legal demand notice through whatsapp on his mobile number 9891638489. He also admitted his signatures on the cheque in Digitally signed AISHWARYA by AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:04:31 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 5 question, however, denied filling it's particulars. He further stated that the complainant has filed this case against him for recovery of the amount and he also stated that he might have returned Rs. 2,000/­ or Rs. 3,000/­ to the complainant but he does not exactly remember the same. He also admitted knowing the complainant and further stated that he intends to make payment and he has brought part payment. The accused stated that he does not wish to lead defence evidence. 9. Final Arguments: Learned counsel for the complainant with the help of Section 118 (a) and Section 139 of the Act argued that complainant has successfully proved guilt of accused for the commission of offence punishable under Section 138 of the Act beyond all reasonable doubt by way of ocular as well as documentary evidence on record. He further argued that though the accused has tried to dispute the financial capacity of the complainant to advance the loan, however, has failed to prove the same, as the complainant stated that she had advanced this amount out of her personal savings and after borrowing some amount from his friend. On the other hand, Learned counsel for the accused argued that complainant has failed to establish the guilt of accused for the commission of offence under Section 138 of the Act beyond all reasonable doubts as the complainant has misused the blank signed cheque of the accused after filling particulars of the same and the amount mentioned in the cheque in question was not due as there was no time fixed for repayment of the amount and the accused has already made part payment of the amount to the complainant. With these submissions, Ld. Counsel for accused has argued that the accused must be acquitted. 10. I have heard both the learned counsels, pursued the material on record and considered the submissions advanced. 11. Appreciation of evidence and finding: Now coming to the merits of the case, I first deem it pertinent to enunciate the law relating to dishonour of cheque. Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:04:36 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 6 12. To bring home a liability under section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, following elements must spring out from the averments in the complaint and the evidence adduced by the complainant, viz, a) A person must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him in a bank for payment of a certain sum of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge of any legally enforceable debt or liability; b) cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier; c) That cheque has been returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with the bank; d) The payee or the holder in due course of the cheque has made a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within 30 days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and e) The drawer of such cheque fails to make payment of the said amount of money to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation: For the purpose of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. 13. Thus, for securing conviction under section 138 of NIA following points are required to be proved: a) The cheque was issued by the drawer in discharge of any debt or other liability. b) It must be legally enforceable debt or liability. Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:04:41 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 7 c) The cheque must be presented by payee within period of 3 months or it's validity whichever is earlier. d) The cheque is dishonoured because of insufficient funds or it exceeds the arrangement. e) A legal notice in writing demanding the payment of cheque is issued within 30 days of the receipt of information from the bank. f) There is default by the drawer to make the payment within 15 days from the date of the receipt of notice. g) The complaint is filed within 30 days from the date of cause of action. 14. Being cumulative, it goes without saying that it is only when all the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied that the person who had drawn the cheque can be deemed to have committed an offence under Section 138 of the Act. 15. Since criminal liability can be attached by proving each element of the Section under which liability is sought to be enforced, I shall now go on to appreciate the evidence­ documentary and oral, in light of how compellingly it satisfies each of such ingredient, if at all. A. A person must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him in a bank for payment of a certain sum of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge of any legally enforceable debt or liability: 16. The first condition pertains to the issuance of the cheque in question to make the payment from an account maintained by the drawer of the cheque towards a legally enforceable debt or other liability. In the present case, the accused has admitted during his statement U/s 313 Cr. P.C and during notice framed U/s 251 Cr. P.C that he had signed the cheque in question, however, he has denied filling Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:04:45 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 8 particulars in the same. With respect to the advancement of loan, the accused has not denied knowing the complainant through Mrs. Pooja and the accused has even admitted during his statement recorded U/S 313 Cr.P.C that he had taken friendly loan of Rs. 35,000/­ from the complainant in the year 2019. Though, the accused has tried to dispute the loan transaction by challenging the financial capacity of the complainant during her cross­examination, however, the complainant in response to the same has stated that she had advanced this amount out of her earning from stitching work and also by borrowing some amount from her friends. The accused has not asked further question or given suggestions to dispute these, which corroborates the story of the complainant regarding advancement of loan in favour of the accused. Further, financial capacity of the complainant also becomes irrelevant considering the admission of the accused that he had received amount of Rs. 35,000/­ from the complainant in the year 2019. Further, the accused during notice put U/S 251 Cr. P.C as well as his statement recorded U/S 313 Cr. P.C has stated that he intends to make the payment to the complainant, which further supports the claim of the complainant that the accused did not return the loan amount taken from the complainant and had given the cheque in question towards the repayment of the same. Though the accused has tried to dispute his liability for payment of the cheque amount by stating during his statement U/S 313 Cr. P.C, that he might have returned Rs. 2,000/­ to Rs. 3,000/­ to the complainant, however, in absence of any documentary evidence or any record of such payment, such version of the accused cannot be believed specifically when the accused did not state so during notice framed U/S 251 Cr. P.C and also keeping in view the fact that the accused has not even specified any date, month and year when such payment was made and further with respect to such payment, the accused has not even given suggestion to CW­1 during her cross­examination. Further, if the accused would have made such payment, the accused must have at least replied to the Digitally signed AISHWARYA by AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:04:58 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 9 legal demand notice of the complainant to dispute his liability but the accused has not even replied to the legal demand notice despite his admission that he has received the amount of Rs. 35,000/­ from the complainant and he has also received legal demand notice from the complainant. The failure of the accused to file reply to the legal demand notice further causes, dubiety to lurk around the story of the defence and adverse, inference can safely be drawn against the accused who has otherwise, failed to adduce any evidence to show that he indeed did everything within his power and control, as a prudent person would do, to ensure that the cheque tendered by him was not misused. Failure, of the accused to prevent such misuse, renders the defence evidence weak. Section 103 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 enunciates that the person who asserts a fact must prove the same unless the law otherwise provides. In the present case, the onus to prove that the accused has not issued the cheque in question to complainant in discharge of any legally enforceable liability rests on the accused, however, the accused has failed to discharge his burden as he has not lead any evidence and further, the accused has also failed to point out any major contradictions or inconsistencies in the testimony of the complainant. 17. The accused has also taken the defence that he has not filled the particulars in the cheque, however, the accused has not given any suggestion to the complainant that he had given blank cheque in question to the complainant or that the complainant had filled the particulars in the cheque in question herself. The accused did not even examine himself to establish this fact. However, even if in absence of any evidence to support the same, we presume for the sake of arguments that blank Cheque had been obtained by Complainant from accused and the contents of the same have not been filled by the accused, the said fact cannot extend any help to accused in the present case. Once the liability of the accused is assessed on record, Complainant was having authority to fill and present said Cheque for encashment as Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:05:08 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 10 when any person issues duly signed blank Cheque to another person, there is implied consent on his behalf, whereby, he gives authority to payee/holder that he may complete Cheque in all respect and present same for payment as per provisions of Section 20 of the NI Act. On this point, I also draw reference from the judgment of Hon'ble Apex Court in case titled as Hon'ble Apex Court in the case titled as Bir Singh v Mukesh Kumar , (2019) 4 SCC 197 wherein it has been held as follows: "...37. A meaningful reading of the provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Act including, in particular, Sections 20 , 87 and 139 , makes it amply clear that a person who signs a cheque and makes it over to the payee remains liable unless he adduces evidence to rebut the presumption that the cheque had been issued for payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability. It is immaterial that the cheque may have been filled in by any person other than the drawer, if the cheque is duly signed by the drawer. If the cheque is otherwise valid, the penal provisions of Section 138 would be attracted. If a signed blank cheque is voluntarily presented to a payee, towards some payment, the payee may fill up the amount and other particulars. This in itself would not invalidate the cheque. The onus would still be on the accused to prove that the cheque was not in discharge of a debt or liability by adducing evidence..." 18. Upon considering the above stated judgment, even accepting the contention of the accused regarding that the fact that the particulars of the cheque in question have not been filled by him to be correct, the said fact will not come to the rescue of the accused as per the binding ratio of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the above stated case, as the same would not invalidate the cheque in question. The onus would still be upon the accused to prove that the cheque in question was not issued in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability, but as discussed above, the Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:05:13 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 11 accused has failed to establish the same. 19. In the present case, the accused has admitted his signature on the cheque in question and he has also admitted that he handed over the cheque in question to the complainant. However, the accused has disputed his liability by claiming that his blank signed cheque which was given as security to the complainant in lieu of amount of Rs. 35,000/­ obtained by him from the complainant in the year 2019 has been misused by the complainant as, there was no time fixed for repayment of the loan amount. Firstly, such submission of the accused is devoid of any oral or documentary evidence and secondly, the same is in contradiction with his own statement, wherein he stated that he had already returned part amount of Rs. 2,000/­ to Rs. 3,000/­ to the complainant. If there was no time fixed for return of the loan amount, there was no occasion for the accused to claim that he repaid part of the amount against the said loan. Further, the accused has tried to dispute his liability by claiming that the cheque in question was given as security, however, this defence of the accused is not tenable as the legal position qua security cheque is no more res­ integra as it has been settled by Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in the case of Credential Leasing & Credits Ltd. v. Shruti Investments & Anr. (2015) 223 DLT 343, wherein after relying upon the case titled as Suresh Chandra Goyal v.Amit Singhal, (2015) 2 DLT (Cri) 803, decided by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi, it was held that: "...15. In Suresh Chandra Goyal Vs. Amit Singhal, Crl . Appeal Nos.601/2015 decided on 14.05.2015, this Court had occasion to consider the defence of "security cheque". In that case the complainant invested monies, from time to time, in the business of the accused. A sum of Rs.3 Lakhs was outstanding after accounting for the monies returned by the accused. The accused entered into a MOU for repayment of the said outstanding amount in 6 monthly Digitally signed by AISHWARYA SHARMA AISHWARYA Date: SHARMA 2023.05.11 15:05:17 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 12 installments of Rs.50,000/ each. The accused issued six security cheques of Rs.50,000/, which were to be returned upon payment of the corresponding installment. While three installments were admittedly received by the complainant, he claimed that the remaining three were not paid. The corresponding security cheques were banked; dishonoured upon presentation, and; after issuance of statutory notice, the complaint under Section 138 NI Act filed due to non payment. This Court, inter alia, observed as follows: 28. There is no magic in the word "security cheque", such that, the moment the accused claims that the dishonoured cheque (in respect whereof a complaint under Section 138 of the Act is preferred) was given as a "security cheque", the Magistrate would acquit the accused. The expression "security cheque" is not a statutorily defined expression in the NI Act . The NI Act does not per se carve out an exception in respect of a "security cheque" to say that a complaint in respect of such a cheque would not be maintainable. There can be mirade situations in which the cheque issued by the accused may be called as security cheque, or may have been issued by way of a security, i.e. to provide an assurance or comfort to the drawee, that in case of failure of the primary consideration on the due date, or on the happening (or not happening) of a contingency, the security may be enforced. While in some situations, the dishonor of such a cheque may attract the penal provisions contained in Section 138 of the Act, in others it may not..." 20. Further, recently, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case titled as APS Forex Services Pvt Ltd v. Shakti International Fashion Linkers and Ors. AIR 2020 SC 945 has held that: "...9. Coming back to the facts in the present case and considering the fact that the accused has admitted the Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:05:22 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 13 issuance of the cheques and his signature on the cheque and that the cheque in question was issued for the second time, after the earlier cheques were dishonoured and that even according to the accused some amount was due and payable, there is a presumption under Section 139 of the N.I. Act that there exists a legally enforceable debt or liability. Of course, such presumption is rebuttable in nature. However, to rebut the presumption the accused was required to lead the evidence that full amount due and payable to the complainant has been paid. In the present case, no such evidence has been led by the accused. The story put forward by the accused that the cheques were given by way of security is not believable in absence of further evidence to rebut the presumption and more particularly the cheque in question was issued for the second time, after the earlier cheques were dishonoured. Therefore, both the courts below have materially erred in not properly appreciating and considering the presumption in favour of the complainant that there exists legally enforceable debt or liability as per Section 139 of the N.I. Act. It appears that both, the Learned Trial Court as well as the High Court, have committed error in shifting the burden upon the complainant to prove the debt or liability, without appreciating the presumption under Section 139 of N.I. Act. As observed above, Section 139 of the Act is an example of reverse onus clause and therefore once the issuance of the cheque has been admitted and even the signature on the cheque has been admitted, there is always a presumption in favour of the complainant that there exists legally enforceable debt or liability and thereafter it is for the accused to rebut such presumption by leading evidence." 21. Thus, the contention of the accused that the cheque in question was given as security cheque finds no force in view of the aforementioned binding judgments of the Hon'ble Courts. Further, since the accused has admitted his signatures on the cheque in question and handing over the cheque in question to the complainant in lieu of loan obtained from the complainant, it becomes necessary to Digitally signed by AISHWARYA SHARMA AISHWARYA Date: SHARMA 2023.05.11 15:05:26 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 14 discuss presumptions in terms of Section 118(a) and Section 139 of the NI Act: (i) Section 118 of the NI Act provides: "Presumptions as to negotiable instruments: Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: (a) of consideration that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;" (ii) Section 139 of the N.I Act further provides as follows: "Presumption in favour of holder it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability". Thus, the combined effect of Section 118 (a) and Section 139 of NI Act raises a presumption in favour of the holder of the cheque that he has received the same for discharge, in whole or in part of any debt or other liability. 22. For appreciating legal position with respect to the presumptions, it is appropriate to refer to the judgement of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee (2001) 6 SCC 16 wherein it was held that: "...22. Because both Sections 138 and 139 require that the Court "shall presume" the liability of the drawer of the cheques for the amounts for which the cheques are drawn, as noted in State of Madras v A. Vaidyanatha Iyer AIR 1958 SC 61, it is obligatory on the Court to raise this presumption in every case where the factual basis for the raising of the presumption had been established. "It introduces an exception to the general rule as to the burden of proof in criminal cases and shifts the onus on to the Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:05:30 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 15 accused". Such a presumption is a presumption of law, as distinguished from a presumption of fact which describes provisions by which the court "may presume" a certain state of affairs. Presumptions are rules of evidence and do not conflict with the presumption of innocence, because by the latter all that is meant is that the prosecution is obliged to prove the case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt. The obligation on the prosecution may be discharged with the help of presumptions of law or fact unless the accused adduces evidence showing the reasonable possibility of the nonexistence of the presumed fact..." 23. Further, recently the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case titled as Kalamani Tex & Anr. v. P. Balasubramanian , 2021 SCC Online SC 75 held that: "...14. Adverting to the case in hand, we find on a plain reading of it's judgment that the trial Court completely overlooked the provisions and failed to appreciate the statutory presumption drawn under Section 118 and Section 139 of NIA. The Statute mandates that once the signature(s) of an accused on the cheque/negotiable instrument are established, then these 'reverse onus' clauses become operative. In such a situation, the obligation shifts upon the accused to discharge the presumption imposed upon him..." 24. From the ratio laid down in the aforesaid judgments, it is clear that for the offence under Section 138 of the Act, the presumptions under Section 118 (a) and Section 139 of NI Act have to be compulsory raised as soon as execution of cheque by accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter, burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. However, a presumption is not in itself evidence but only makes a prima facie case for a party for whose benefit it exists. These presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of NI Act are rebuttable in nature. 25. In the present case, the accused has admitted his signature on the cheque in Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:05:35 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 16 question. Thus, the presumption as mentioned above, is raised in favour of the complainant and now onus is upon the accused to rebut the said presumption. With respect to the rebuttal, it is pertinent to refer to the judgment of the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of M/s Kumar Exports v Sharma Carpets , (2009) 2 SCC 513, wherein it was held that: "...20. The accused in a trial under Section 138 of the Act has two options. He can either show that consideration and debt did not exist or that under the circumstances of the case the non­existence of consideration and debt is so probable that a prudent man ought to suppose that no consideration and debt existed. To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the Court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the nonexistence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not serve the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the Court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their nonexistence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. Apart from adducing direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence and if the circumstances so relied Digitally signed AISHWARYA by AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:05:40 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 17 upon are compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on the complainant. The accused may also rely upon presumptions of fact, for instance, those mentioned in Section 114 of the Evidence Act to rebut the presumptions arising under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act..." 26. Further, the above said principles have also been recently crystallized by Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Basalingappa v Mudibasappa , (2019) 5 SCC 418, which is as follows: "...25. We having noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in above cases on Sections 118(a) and 139 , we now summarise the principles enumerated by this Court in following manner: (i) Once the execution of cheque is admitted Section 139 of the Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. (ii) The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. (iii) To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. (iv) That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence, Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. (v) It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence..." Thus, as per the presumptions raised under the NI Act , the burden to raise a probable defence lies upon the accused, however, the accused has simple denied his liability but has not lead any oral or documentary evidence to establish his defences, thus, the version of the accused cannot be relied upon. On this point, it is relevant to refer to the judgment pronounced by the Hon'ble Parent High Court in V.S. Yadav v Reena, CRL. A. NO. 1136 Of 2010, wherein it was held that: "...Mere pleading not guilty and stating that the cheques were issued as security, would not give amount to rebutting the presumption raised under Section 139 of N.I. Act. If mere statement under Section 313 Cr. P.C. or under Section 281 Cr. P.C. of accused of pleading not guilty was sufficient to rebut the entire evidence produced by the complainant/ prosecution, then every accused has to be acquitted. But, it is not the law. In order to rebut the presumption under Section 139 of N.I. Act, the accused, by cogent evidence, has to prove the circumstance under which cheques were issued. It was for the accused to prove if no loan was taken why he did not write a letter to the complainant for return of the cheque. Unless the accused had proved that he acted like a normal businessman/prudent person entering into a contract he could not have rebutted the presumption u/s 139 N.I. Act. If no loan was given, but cheques were retained, he immediately would have protested and asked the cheques to be returned and if still cheques were not returned, he would have served a notice as complainant. Nothing was proved in this case..." 28. In view of the discussion made above, it becomes clear that in the present case the complainant has successfully established that she had extended the loan of Rs. 35,000/­ to the accused and the same was not repaid by the accused and in discharge of the said liability, the accused had issued the cheque in question in favour of the complainant. The accused has not been able to rebut the presumption existing in favour of the complainant by either leading evidence or by pointing out any Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2023.05.11 15:05:51 +0530 CC NI Act.7822/2021 Raj Bala Vs. Gurpreet Singh Page No. 19 material inconsistencies or contradictions in the statement of CW­1. Therefore, considering the weight of the attending circumstances viz, the consistency in the prosecution story, the compelling documentary evidence adduced by the complainant and since, that the accused has not proved his defence to cause the probabilities to lie in his favour, the first element of Section 138 NI Act stands assembled. B. That cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of it's validity whichever is earlier: 29. As far as this condition is concerned, the same is satisfied upon the perusal of the cheque in question EX. CW­1/A dated 20.11.2020 and the return memo EX. CW1/B dt. 21.11.2020. The return memo clearly shows that the cheque in question has been presented within the prescribed period of limitation. Thus, this ingredient also stands satisfied. C. That cheque has been returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of the account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with the bank: 30. In the present case, the cheque in question upon presentation was dishonored due to insufficient funds in the account of the accused, as shown in the return memo EX. CW1/B dt. 21.11.2020. The defence did not adduce any evidence whatsoever to contradict the same. The accused has even admitted the correctness of dishonour of the cheque in question during his statement U/S 313 Cr. P.C and also in his admission/ denial statement recorded U/S 294 Cr. P.C. Such admission of the accused clearly shows that he issued cheque from the account in question intentionally despite being aware that the same will not be honoured. As far as the making of demand by sending a legal notice is concerned, the complainant had sent the legal notice EX. Thus, the receipt of legal notice to accused is sufficient to fulfil the criteria as required for the offence under section 138 NI Act. Thus, the fourth condition, to entail liability under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is fulfilled. E. The last condition is that the accused fails to make the payment within fifteen days from the date of the receipt of the legal demand notice. In the present case, the accused has evidently failed to make the payment within fifteen days. Thus, the last limb of what will entail the liability against the accused is also structured. 33. Ratio: In the instant case, it was the sole burden and duty of accused to prove absence of liability by raising a ''probable'' defence as the presumption of law operates in favour of existence of debt or liability.
